messages.author: b1e64236b865525c
messages.subject: Additive or multiplicative error terms
parts:
This may be a very basic question, but here it is, anyway:
When dealing with strictly positive variables, people often use multiplicative error terms (with mean = 1 for the same reason that mean = 0 in additive error terms).
But there are at least two ways to write that in our model: using (for example) a lognormal distribution for Y / expected_Y, or using a normal distribution (centered at zero) for log (Y) - log (expected_Y). Yes they are mathematically equivalent, but is there any computational argument in favor of one over the other when it comes to Stan models?
Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Additive or multiplicative error terms
parts:
They're not quite the same. You get the Jacobian
adjustment in the lognormal, which will matter if
your Y is a parameter. See the x in the denominator of
the pdf defined here:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution

If Y is a constant, then that term gets dropped out if
you're using the sampling notation but not if you call
lognormal_lpdf(...) [as you would in a mixture model].

For efficiency, they're not much different. There's
the extra log calculation, which you'd only want to do
once. Then it's very similar up to the Jacobian adjustment.

There's also the transform if you have a positive constrained
location parameter mu (your expected_Y) or if you have
Y as parameter (as opposed to log Y). In these cases, it
can be a bit more efficient to work on the unconstrained (log)
scale and then exp() up to the constrained positive scale
after the fact.

But I wouldn't worry about the efficiency difference for
these.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Additive or multiplicative error terms
parts:
Hi Bob! First of all, thanks for being so helpful.
I think I understand your reply, and I think I understand what you write here ("Jacobian Adjustments"): http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
That said, I'm afraid I could have been more explicit about the two options I'm considering.
My dependent variable y is strictly positive, and I want to model it using an independent variable x (which, by the way, is non-negative) and a functional form f with parameters (say) a1 and a2.
I also have a vector of weights, since each x-y occurs in a number of observations (assumed to be iid). So I had two options in mind (see below), and wanted to know (a) whether they are truly equivalent and (b) whether one is much more efficient than the other. I'm guessing your response to (b) is no, but now I'm not sure about (a) anymore...
Thanks!

...
transformed parameters {
    real mean_log_y;
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        mean_log_y [i] = f (x [i], a1, a2); // This is not actual Stan code, of course
    }
}
model {
    a1 ~ ...;
    a2 ~ ...;
    sigma ~ ...; // Some strictly positive distribution
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        target += weight [i] * normal_lpdf (log_y [i] | mean_log_y [i], sigma);
    }
}

...
transformed parameters {
    real mean_log_y;
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        mean_log_y [i] = f (x [i], a1, a2); // This is not actual Stan code, of course
    }
}
model {
    a1 ~ ...;
    a2 ~ ...;
    sigma ~ ...; // Some strictly positive distribution
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        target += weight [i] * lognormal_lpdf (y [i] | mean_log_y [i] - sigma * sigma / 2, sigma); // I write it like this just so that the distribution has mean exp (mean_log_y)
    }
}
